title: Lawful excuse
label: DPP v Ziegler · 2021
summary: The Supreme Court held that blocking a road in protest can be lawful if prosecution would be disproportionate. Later cases confined that reading, and a different "lawful excuse" in the Criminal Damage Act turns on belief in consent, not on the merits of the cause.
rule: It is an offence to wilfully obstruct a highway "without lawful authority or excuse" (Highways Act 1980, section 137). In *DPP v Ziegler* (2021) the Supreme Court held that when protest rights under Articles 10 and 11 are engaged, whether there was a lawful excuse can turn on whether a conviction would be proportionate. It restored the acquittals of protesters who had blocked a road.
nuance: "Lawful excuse" is not one defence. *Ziegler* is about the words in the Highways Act. The Criminal Damage Act 1971 has its own section 5. A result under one does not travel to the other.

*Ziegler* was widely read as making proportionality a defence to any protest offence. The Supreme Court later said that reading was mistaken. Where Parliament has already struck the balance in the offence itself, there is no further case-by-case proportionality element.
In *DPP v Cuciurean* (March 2022) the Divisional Court held that a conviction for aggravated trespass is proportionate in itself, with no separate assessment needed.

In the Colston statue reference (September 2022) the Court of Appeal held that violent or non-peaceful conduct falls outside Articles 9, 10 and 11, so proportionality does not arise. Prosecution for significant damage to property could not be a disproportionate interference even where the protest was otherwise peaceful. Minor or transient damage can still require a fact-specific question. The reference did not affect the acquittals.

A second lawful excuse, in section 5(2)(a) of the Criminal Damage Act, is an honest belief that the owner would have consented had they known of the damage and its circumstances. In Attorney General's Reference (No 1 of 2023) the Court of Appeal held that those circumstances can include the time, place and extent of the damage, and the fact that it was done as a protest against a particular cause. They do not include the merits, urgency or importance of the cause, or the defendant's wider reasons. Evidence about those matters is not admissible for this defence. That reference, too, left the acquittal standing.
*Ziegler* still matters where the offence includes a lawful-excuse ingredient and the protest is peaceful, as with obstructing a highway.
why_it_matters: Whether proportionality is a live question decides whether a jury or magistrate weighs the protester's rights at all.

history.text: *DPP v Ziegler*: the Supreme Court restores the protesters' acquittals.
*DPP v Cuciurean*: no separate proportionality assessment for aggravated trespass.
Colston statue reference: violent or non-peaceful conduct falls outside Convention protection, and significant damage cannot make a conviction disproportionate. The acquittals stand.
Northern Ireland safe access zones reference: the Supreme Court says the wide reading of *Ziegler* was mistaken.
Attorney General's Reference (No 1 of 2023): the merits of a protest are not "circumstances" of the damage for the consent defence in section 5(2)(a). The acquittal is unaffected.
